tutorial_text:
1. Shoot in a well-lit place.

2. Keep the photo sharp.

3. Frame the snake's BODY, not just the head. Identification relies on the body pattern.

4. Use the gallery if you prefer.

Keep a safe distance!

Recognition was trained on the species with enough photos, and the entries came from a survey of snakes recorded in Brazil, so the two lists do not fully overlap. medical_disclaimer_text:
Get to the nearest emergency room. Bring a photo of the animal if you have one.

Take off rings, bracelets and anything tight on the bitten side: the area swells fast. Keep the person lying down and still, with the bitten arm or leg higher than the rest of the body.

No tourniquet, no cutting, no sucking the venom out, nothing applied on top.

Tell the doctor what you saw and show the photo. The antivenom is chosen from that and from the symptoms that appear, so describe what the person is feeling.

no_snake_found_message:
Automatic detection didn't locate the snake in this photo. This usually happens when the animal is far away, camouflaged or poorly lit, and it doesn't necessarily mean there is no snake in the image.

You can identify it anyway. Species recognition is a separate step and often succeeds even when detection fails.

disclaimer_short: Don't decide on this result alone. If someone is bitten, get medical care right away.
disclaimer_short_low: This species has no fangs to inject venom. The app can be wrong, so when in doubt, ask a specialist.
disclaimer_short_medium: Brazil's Ministry of Health classes this as a snake of no public health importance. Get medical care if the reaction gets worse.
medium_disclaimer_text:
Brazil's Ministry of Health separates the snakes of public health importance, which are lanceheads, rattlesnakes, bushmasters and coral snakes, from all the others. Rear-fanged snakes fall outside that group, and no antivenom exists for them.

The fangs sit at the back of the mouth, so injecting takes a prolonged bite. When it happens, the reaction stays around the bite: pain, swelling, redness, sometimes numbness, bruising or a swollen lymph node nearby. It usually improves within days.

Wash with soap and water, take off rings and bracelets on the bitten side, and keep watching. Get medical care if the swelling spreads, the pain grows or bleeding appears.

These signs resemble a pit viper bite, and the app may have got the species wrong. If you do see a doctor, describe the symptoms: treatment is decided from those and from what you saw of the animal.
low_disclaimer_text:
With no injecting fangs, the bite is a wound like any other: wash it with soap and water and keep it clean. Watch for spreading redness, pus or fever, which are signs of infection, not venom.

The app may have got the species wrong. If it swells a lot or hurts far more than a bite should, get medical care and describe the symptoms.
consent_text: This app uses artificial intelligence to suggest the species, and it can be wrong. It is there to learn from and to give you a lead, not to decide treatment. If someone is bitten, get medical care right away.
consent_checkbox: I understand the identification may be incorrect.
poisonous_info_body:
People use the two words interchangeably, but they don't mean the same thing.

Venomous is an animal that can inject its toxin, through fangs or a stinger. Snakes belong here: the danger is in the bite.

Poisonous is one that carries the toxin but has no way to inject it. It only harms you if eaten or touched, like pufferfish and some frogs.

So, strictly speaking, no Brazilian snake is poisonous. If you came looking for that word, this is the right entry.
ai_confidence_info_body:
It is how sure the model is about the species it picked.

Worth knowing: it understates itself. We tested it on 250 photos, and when the number sat around 50% the species was right 71% of the time. Above 80%, it got every one right.

So a middling value doesn't mean it failed. If it drops below 60%, have a look at the other possibilities at the bottom of the page: the right species shows up in the top three in 9 out of 10 cases.

None of this replaces medical care if someone is bitten.
